digest.definition: Geography studies how societies and environments shape each other, through the lenses of scale, place, space and time
distinctiveFeatures: Geography studies how societies and environments shape each other, through the lenses of scale, place, space and time
It is at once a STEM and a SHAPE subject, joining natural and social sciences with arts and humanities, and courses run as BA, BSc, Scottish MA and integrated master's
It values plural ways of knowing, qualitative and quantitative, and rests on fieldwork, laboratory work, spatial data analysis, modelling, GIS and remote sensing
It sees itself as an inclusive learning community that must face its colonial origins and carry values of care and solidarity through the whole curriculum
Fieldwork, in an expansive sense of the field from landscapes to archives and digital spaces, is required throughout the degree
Geocapabilities, the subject's own capabilities of thinking spatially and holistically about place, society and environment, grow as students progress

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: A collective duty to embed equity and inclusion, framed by the discipline's colonial past; carried into curriculum values, critical theory and inclusive fieldwork and partnerships (D1, 1.5 to 1.9; 2.6; 2.15; 3.19)

Inclusive design across teaching, assessment and above all fieldwork, with affordable trips, flexible delivery and allowance for unequal access to technology (D1, 2.3 to 2.6; 2.11 to 2.13; 3.19; 3.40)
Sustainable development is core content and a rung row; fieldwork carries a carbon audit; three principles from the ESD guidance shape teaching (D1, 1.10; 3.20; 4.5; 4.8)

Employability, entrepreneurship and enterprise read broadly: data and spatial skills for decisions, and social, green and digital enterprise valued beside economic surplus (D1, 1.11; 1.12; 2.14; 3.34)

statements.appliesTo: everyone in the geography learning community
statements.about: a shared duty to embed equity and inclusion
statements.paraphrase: The subject community has a shared duty, going past legal minimums, to build equity, equality, diversity and inclusion into its institutions, curricula and teaching, for example by widening participation, countering under-representation, refusing discrimination and closing awarding gaps; everyone in it will need to engage, reflect and change to meet that duty.

forPractitioner.text: Treat inclusion as a task for the whole community: staff, students and partners will need to engage, reflect and change, with concrete work on widening participation, under-represented groups, zero tolerance of harassment, neurodiverse access and awarding gaps.

forBeneficiary.text: As a member of the geography learning community you will be asked to help make it fair and inclusive: to take part, reflect on your own assumptions and be ready to change.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: the geography learning community
statements.paraphrase: Because the discipline's knowledge grew partly out of colonial science that helped justify empire, its colonial and imperial legacies of systemic disadvantage, such as racism, classism, ableism, homophobia and patriarchy, must be acknowledged and countered through a learning community that includes everyone involved.

forPractitioner.text: Course teams must name and actively work against the colonial roots of geographical knowledge and their present-day legacies of disadvantage, building a community that includes students, academics, technicians, professional staff, visitors and partners.

forBeneficiary.text: You will look at how geography's colonial past still shapes disadvantage today, and you belong to a community that must recognise and work against those legacies.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: the geography curriculum
statements.about: core values across the whole curriculum
statements.paraphrase: The inclusive community rests on care for people and places, respect for other views and ways of life, attention to decolonial demands and solidarity against injustice; these values should run through the whole curriculum rather than sit in single modules or sub-fields.

forPractitioner.text: Thread care, plural knowledges, respect, decolonial attention and solidarity through every part of the curriculum; they should not be confined to particular modules or sub-fields.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design; the student meets its effect across modules

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: the geography curriculum
statements.paraphrase: The core values favour curricula that build critical thinking from progressive theory, among them critical race theory, decoloniality, disability, feminist and queer studies and science and technology studies; critical theory should be applied across geography, and the values also favour design that anticipates the barriers of each learning site, fieldwork and laboratories above all.

forPractitioner.text: Apply critical theory across every branch of the course, not only in human geography, and plan each learning site, whether online, in a classroom, outdoors or in a laboratory, with its likely barriers anticipated.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: data skills for innovation and enterprise
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will be able to gather, analyse and handle varied numerical and qualitative data; their spatial analysis, crossing scales and disciplines, lets them tackle complex social and economic problems and use evidence for innovation and decisions, and they see the worth of alternative economies and of green, social and digital entrepreneurship.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will collect, analyse and work with quantitative and qualitative data, bring spatial analysis across scales and disciplines to complex social and economic problems, and use evidence to inform innovation and decisions, understanding green, social and digital enterprise.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to collect, analyse and work with both numerical and qualitative data, use your spatial thinking to help solve complex social and economic problems, and understand different kinds of enterprise, including green, social and digital ones.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: Geography courses
statements.paraphrase: Geography degrees aim at an integrative education; courses should rest on learning outcomes that grow in complexity and match teaching and assessment, with design led by subject experts and shaped by student engagement and co-creation.

forPractitioner.text: Design the course so its outcomes rise in complexity year on year and line up with how you teach and assess, and involve students in reviewing and co-producing the design.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: fieldwork leaders and course designers
statements.paraphrase: Fieldwork needs access to many kinds of field; essential as it is, students' individual needs during fieldwork should be recognised, fieldwork leaders are responsible for anticipatory design so that no field site excludes anyone on any protected characteristic, class, gender identity or neurodiversity and facilities suffice, and designers need to stop the extra costs of travel, clothing and kit from barring anyone.

forPractitioner.text: Recognise students' individual needs in the field; fieldwork leaders are responsible for anticipating barriers of any protected characteristic, class, gender identity or neurodiversity and for adequate facilities, and course designers need to keep extra fieldwork, clothing or equipment costs from excluding anyone.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on fieldwork leaders and course designers; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: students at the end of the course
statements.about: placing a specialism within the wider discipline
statements.paraphrase: Study grows more specialised as the degree goes on, after a broad first grounding; by the end, students will be able to place their chosen specialisms within a wider grasp of geography, its approach, history and theory, and applicants need clear information on what each course offers.

forPractitioner.text: Build breadth early and specialism later, so that by the end students will situate their specialism within geography's wider approach, history and theory; tell applicants clearly what is distinctive about your course.

forBeneficiary.text: Your degree will start broad and let you specialise later; by the end you will be able to show how your specialism fits into geography as a whole, including its history and theory.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: students as they progress
statements.paraphrase: As they progress, students are able to judge evidence and the value of their sources with growing sophistication; they will have chances to show deeper critical reflection and will show a growing capacity to carry out fieldwork or projects on their own with primary or secondary data.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for growth: students will evaluate evidence and sources with rising sophistication, will be given chances to show deeper critical reflection, and will take on fieldwork or projects with increasing independence.

forBeneficiary.text: As you move through your degree you will judge evidence and sources more critically, and you will be able to plan and carry out fieldwork or projects more and more on your own.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: students as they progress, and their courses
statements.about: how collecting data shapes knowledge of the world
statements.paraphrase: As they progress, students should come to understand more fully how the epistemology of collecting primary data affects what we take the world to be, and should have chances to grasp better how data relate to the real world and to geographical knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: Give students chances, as they progress, to see how collecting primary data shapes knowledge of the world and how data relate to reality; students should deepen this understanding over the course.

forBeneficiary.text: As you progress, you should come to understand how the way data are collected shapes what we think we know about the world.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: course design and resourcing
statements.about: resourcing flexible material and unequal access to technology
statements.paraphrase: Accessible, inclusive and flexible material needs extra resources to keep quality high, and design should allow for students' unequal access to technology so that flexibility does not cause harm nobody planned.

forPractitioner.text: Resource flexible and accessible materials properly, and design them to work for students with limited devices or connectivity, so that flexibility does not backfire.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design and resourcing

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Geography degree

statements.appliesTo: institutions
statements.paraphrase: Institutions should make sure every student has an equal chance to take part in partnerships where relevant; partnerships inside the institution, such as societies and work across departments, count as much as external ones, and partners take on the same equity duties.

forPractitioner.text: Make partnership opportunities, from placements and projects to student societies, equally open to all students, and brief partners on the equity, equality, diversity and inclusion principles they share with you.

statements.appliesTo: partnership activities
statements.paraphrase: Partnerships may cross disciplines, institutions and sectors and may be brief or lasting; they should be designed around students and help them understand the subject beyond their studies.

statements.appliesTo: providers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance; providers will use external reviewers in periodic review to get an outside view of proposed changes and to check that threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Bring external reviewers into periodic review to test proposed changes, confirm threshold standards are met and check the content fits geography.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in quality assurance

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: spatial distributions and change across scales
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will be able to show knowledge and explanation of how physical and human phenomena are distributed in space; they grasp change at different scales of time and space, judge the processes shaping past, present and future geographies, and see how the chosen scale affects conclusions.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will show knowledge and explanation of spatial distributions in physical and human phenomena, understand rates of change across scales, evaluate the processes behind past, present and future geographies, and recognise how scale shapes conclusions.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to explain where physical and human things are found and why, how they change over time and space, and how the scale you study at affects what you conclude.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: systems thinking about human and natural worlds
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will be able to use systems thinking to frame patterns, processes, interactions and change critically in a world of people, biodiversity and geodiversity, taking in environmental effects on people, human effects on natural and climate systems, and environmental management.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will apply a systems framework to think critically about patterns, processes and change, taking in environmental impacts on people, human impacts on biophysical and climate systems, and the management of environments.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to use systems thinking to understand how people and the natural world affect each other, climate included, and how environments are managed.

statements.appliesTo: Geography degrees and their students
statements.paraphrase: Fieldwork, mixing directed, peer and self-directed learning with extended time in the field including multi-day and residential trips, is required across the whole degree so that core skills can progress, often ending in self-directed fieldwork; it builds teamwork, problem-based learning, research design, data handling, resilience and the handling of risk, and it alone links the real world to its measurement in spatial data.

forPractitioner.text: Include fieldwork at every stage of the degree, with extended and residential time in the field, so that core skills progress, typically to self-directed fieldwork by the end; this is a requirement, not an option.

forBeneficiary.text: You will do fieldwork throughout your degree, including longer and residential trips, building up to planning your own fieldwork by the end.

statements.appliesTo: those who plan and run taught fieldwork
statements.about: ethics and risk assessment before fieldwork
statements.paraphrase: Fieldwork invites reflection on positionality, responsibility and relationships, so all fieldwork should be planned and run ethically, responsibly, carefully and safely for everyone involved, with an ethics assessment and a risk assessment before any taught fieldwork.

forPractitioner.text: Complete an ethics assessment and a risk assessment before every taught field trip, and plan it to be ethical, responsible, careful and safe for students, staff, the communities visited and other stakeholders.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on those who plan fieldwork; the student meets its effect

statements.appliesTo: those who plan fieldwork, and providers
statements.paraphrase: Fieldwork should be planned and run to be inclusive and accessible, minding students' and staff's wellbeing and all protected characteristics; opportunities should be fair, providers should, as far as they can, fund their way round cost and other barriers, and an inclusivity impact assessment should come before all taught fieldwork.

forPractitioner.text: Plan every field trip for inclusion and access, mental and physical health included; fund ways round cost barriers where you can, and complete an inclusivity impact assessment beforehand.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider and fieldwork planners

statements.appliesTo: those who plan taught fieldwork
statements.paraphrase: The environmental impact and carbon footprint of fieldwork should be weighed through a carbon audit before all taught fieldwork; destinations and transport should be justified by programme outcomes, setting environmental cost against the learning and other gains of studying in a place.

forPractitioner.text: Run a carbon audit before each taught trip and justify the destination and travel by the outcomes they serve, weighing carbon cost against learning gains.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on fieldwork planners

statements.appliesTo: the provider as employer of fieldwork staff
statements.about: training and capacity of fieldwork staff
statements.paraphrase: Staff carry heavy responsibility in taught fieldwork; the provider's resourcing should make sure they are fully trained and supported, and employers must recognise that staff differ in their capacity to lead or join fieldwork.

forPractitioner.text: Resource and train fieldwork staff fully; as employer you must recognise that colleagues differ in how far they can lead or take part in fieldwork.
